newsitem.title: GERMANY: SOCCER-GERMAN TV BOSSES CALL FOR MORE BREAKS IN GAMES.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-GERMAN TV BOSSES CALL FOR MORE BREAKS IN GAMES.

text.p: The bosses of two of Germany's leading private television stations want soccer matches divided into thirds or even quarters to allow for more advertising.
One of them said he had discussed the proposal with FIFA general secretary Sepp Blatter, whom he claimed was receptive to the idea.

Despite huge audience ratings and lively interest among TV advertisers in both German league and European games, the channels say they cannot make a profit because of the fees they pay for broadcasting rights.

"The only way of financing it is to break the game up into thirds," Sat1 managing director Fred Kogel was quoted as saying by the Bild am Sonntag newspaper. Kogel called for two 10-minute breaks between the three periods.
"There is a danger that in a few years it will only be possible to show soccer on pay-TV, and a large part of the audience will be shut out for financial reasons," he said.

Helmut Thoma, head of RTL television which has German rights to the European Cup, said managers should be able to call two time-outs of two or three minutes in each half, which could be used to show commercials.
Thoma urged German football authorities to take the issue to FIFA and said he had discussed the matter with Blatter. "The chances are good," he said.
"This is the only way to provide the viewers with a comprehensive supply of the expensive commodity that soccer has become," Thoma said.
German club officials generally welcomed the idea.
"Two breaks would allow the players to recover much better physically, and the coaches would have more tactical possibilities," said Gerd Niebaum, president of champions Borussia Dortmund.
Bayer Leverkusen manager Reiner Calmund said: "Interruptions don't hurt the suspense of a match."
But Werder Bremen manager Willi Lemke told Radio Bremen sport had to be extremely careful not to adapt exclusively to the interests of sponsors and the media.
